title: Davie Tough and Baby Dodds as influences
summary: Leeman names Catlett, Zutty Singleton, Davie Tough and Baby Dodds, whom he heard at the Three Deuces in 1939, and describes Dodds's rolls, open bass drum and tricks.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: In our previous session, interview session, Milt, we went to great lengths on Jo Jones and his impact on my drum, his impact on me drumnistically. But there are other very important things that affected my plan and eventually help me to adopt my own style of playing and expression.

Next to Jo Jones, I would say Sidney Catlett, then possible Zutty Singleton along the way. I'll get to each one eventually. There was Davie Tough, all 110 pounds of him ringing wet! He was a great swinger. And equally as powerful. I have had some people compare my approach to his in a certain period in my life. His was not to predominate the soloist, but to feed them. His big band work with

Woody Herman showed how exciting he could feed without getting in the way of the soloist and the arrangements. I was -- to hear over the years, Baby Dodds, who like Zutty Singleton, came north to Chicago out of New Orleans via the riverboats. Their's was a pulsating, four four beat of the traditional Orleans style. Baby Dodds played with the original Three Deuces in 1939 when I had the chance to hear him and to study his approach.

He worked at the bar with the Deuces with -- did I mention 1939? Yes. He worked with at that time Louie Armstrong on piano and the fabulous -- to me, fabulous -- Lonnie Johnson on guitar, a truly great blues guitarist, blues vocalist. I've been hearing what used to be called race records then, I used to get a hold of everything I could get my hands on, and in that idiom, and I guess that meant predominantly black artists, the race record title that is, because some blue, racy, or possibly offensive material was on them in those days, and most of them were found in juke boxes around the south and the midwest and in bars and so forth.

Anyway, Baby Dodds had a roll and snare drum, so artistically smooth it was referred to as smooth as silk or satin. He played, as did Zutty Singleton, with the open tone of the base drum. They tuned the base drum, but no padding in the heads and vibrating free. Baby Dodds employed all kinds of little tricks in his solos, using

tom toms and bass drums, the butt end of the sticks, etc. on the bass drum, making a tom tom sound. And with the wood blocks and the rims of the bass drum, one heavy cymbal, his breaks were like Zutty -- the same approach on drums, but they were most amusing, very amusing.
